name: Revisionism
summary: Revisionism is Eduard Bernstein's revision of Marxism in the German Social Democratic Party around 1896-1914. It rejects the expected collapse of capitalism, growing immiseration and the dictatorship of the proletariat, and holds that socialism is reached step by step through democracy, universal suffrage, trade unions, consumer co-operatives and municipal reform, with democracy as both its means and its substance. Bernstein called socialists the heirs of liberalism, put ethics beside economic necessity, accepted national defence and a reformed colonial policy, and later condemned Bolshevik dictatorship.
scope: Bernstein's revisionism as its defining sources describe it: Steger's encyclopedia entry, Engehausen's account of the 'Revisionismusstreit' and the German History in Documents abstract all present it as Bernstein's critique of Marxist theory and tactics from 1896, set out in Die Voraussetzungen des Sozialismus (Evolutionary Socialism), which Bernstein himself calls an exposition of the German social democratic revisionists' tendencies. Sources used: that book, Bernstein's articles of the revisionist debate and after (1896 replies to Bax, 1907 on patriotism, 1915 'Revisionism and Nationalism', 1922 on Bolshevism), and the immediate demands of the Erfurt programme, which Bernstein co-drafted and says he does not want to change. Excluded: the Erfurt programme's theoretical part, which he rejected; other revisionists where they differed from him; Bernstein's writings before 1896; the later pejorative uses of 'revisionism' by Leninists, Maoists and Soviet theorists; reformism and post-war social democracy, which are separate subjects.

notes: Later pass (claude-opus-5-5, 2026-11-09) bringing a pre-rules audit up to rules 5. The first pass rested partly on two Wikipedia articles (s5, s6), which are kept only for the review history; answers that rested on them, or on a general value such as 'democracy is the substance of socialism' that does not settle the statement, were re-sourced from Bernstein's own texts or nulled (reviewHistory keeps the earlier versions). Themes searched: economy (ownership, co-operatives, municipal enterprise, taxation, welfare and the right to work, value theory, crises, trade), government (suffrage, representation, direct legislation, federalism and municipal autonomy, dictatorship, revolution), world (nation, patriotism, colonies, war, arbitration, international law), society and liberty (religion, free expression, women's legal equality), and culture, ecology and technology, on which the revisionist texts are silent. The Erfurt programme's immediate demands are used because Bernstein co-drafted them and states in Evolutionary Socialism that he does not wish to change them, noting only doubts about free legal services; they are answered at medium confidence. Bernstein's colonial views (a 'higher right' of higher civilisation, a reformed socialist colonial policy) are recorded as stated, as Haag's FES article describes the revisionist current. Not used: Bernstein's 1890 and 1895 articles (before the revisionist debate), his 1897 essays on Marx (about Marx's views), and the hostile accounts of Lenin, Luxemburg and later anti-revisionists. The Dictionary of the History of Ideas entry 'Marxist Revisionism' (Kindersley) could not be reached (the University of Virginia host returned no content). The original 'Problems of Socialism' articles and Bernstein's later Reichstag speeches were not found as open full text. Critics, notably Maoists, used 'revisionism' pejoratively for any deviation from orthodoxy; those uses are other subjects.
